title: Stochastic trust-region and direct-search methods: A weak tail bound condition and reduced sample sizing
contribution: A single power-law tail bound on the estimated decrease (not on each function estimate), scaled by the sufficient-decrease power q > 1. It cuts per-iteration samples from O(Delta_k^-4) to O(Delta_k^-2q) for q in (1,2] (O(Delta_k^-2-eps) as q -> 1), or to O(Delta_k^-eps) with common random numbers. It gives almost-sure Clarke stationarity for simple stochastic direct-search and trust-region methods on nonsmooth f.
problem_entry: Starts from a cost in the literature: stochastic TR/DS methods need O(Delta^-4) samples per iteration with decrease power 2. A second gap is that model-based stochastic DFO needs accurate gradient estimates, which are unavailable for nonsmooth f (pp. 2-4).
key_idea: Put the probabilistic condition on the reduction estimate used in the acceptance test, at scale alpha*Delta_k^q, and couple the sample size to q. The DS and TR skeletons (Basic DFO-TRNS) are kept; exact values become estimates and the power 2 becomes q (pp. 3-6, 10, 15).
assumptions: Assumption 2.1: P(|estimate error of the decrease| >= alpha*Delta^q | F_{k-1}) <= eps_q/alpha^{q/(q-1)}, with a known bound on eps_q and theta above a threshold (3.1). Sample bounds need a finite r-th noise moment, r = q/(q-1), and i.i.d. averaging; the CRN route needs a known generator and correlated errors (2.10). Theorems also need f locally Lipschitz, bounded iterates and dense directions on unsuccessful iterations; TR needs ||B_k|| <= ||G_k||/(rho*Delta_k) (pp. 5-8, 11, 13, 15).
proof_devices: potential Phi_k = f(X_k) - f* + eta*Delta_k^q with eta = theta/taubar_q; E[Phi_k - Phi_{k+1} | F_{k-1}] >= eps*Delta_k^q implies sum E[Delta_k^q] < inf (Thm 3.1, pp. 11-12)
false-success loss bound: write true decrease as (theta - Z_k)Delta_k^q; success implies estimate error >= Z_k*Delta_k^q, so the tail bound caps the expected loss at eps_f*Delta_k^q (p. 12)
Lemma 2.3: tail bound extended from constant alpha to an F_{k-1}-measurable random threshold via discrete approximation, Beppo Levi and dominated convergence (pp. 6-7)
Borel-Cantelli on sum P(error >= Delta_k/m) <= m^r eps_q sum E[Delta_k^q] < inf, then Clarke-derivative argument on unsuccessful iterations with dense directions (Lemma 3.2, Thm 3.3, pp. 12-14)
TR transfer via ||S_k|| >= rho*Delta_k from a Hessian bound (Lemma 4.2, p. 16); asymptotic alignment S_k -> -G_k (Prop. 4.8, p. 18)
sample sizes via Markov on the r-th moment of an average with Rosenthal (r >= 2) or von Bahr-Esseen (1 < r < 2) inequalities (App. A.1, pp. 26-28)
rival conditions imply the new one: conditional Chebyshev (Prop. 2.10) and event inclusion (2.14) (Prop. 2.12) (p. 9, pp. 29-30)
experiments: 96 nonsmooth problems x 10 runs (|P| = 960). Data and performance profiles on evaluations built on the true f, budget 10000(n+1), gamma in {1e-2, 1e-4}, Gaussian noise sd 0.1. q = 1.5 beats q = 2. SDS+1.5 and STR1.5 beat StoMADS. Theta = 0.5 was tuned although the theory requires theta > 4 (or about 9), which is disclosed in Remark 5.2 (pp. 19-23, 30).
positioning: Re-states the model-based (Larson-Billups, ASTRO-DF, Chen-Menickelly-Scheinberg) and direct-search (Dzahini, StoMADS) lines, and proves their accuracy conditions imply the new one. It borrows Dzahini's supermartingale conclusion and criticizes rivals only for needing gradient estimates unavailable for nonsmooth f (pp. 2-4, 9, 11).
writing: Headline sample counts are in the abstract, followed by a contributions subsection and a single priority claim ('first time', p. 4). Proofs go to the appendix. The numerics are hedged and a conjecture is labelled as one. There are editing slips (leftover appendix sentence p. 7, 'common number generator' p. 8) (pp. 1-8, 20-23).
limits_future: Stated limits: the eps_q bound must be known, the theoretical theta is unusable in practice, and the iteration-complexity price of q -> 1 is open. There are no rates and no code. Future work: nonsmooth random models (piecewise linear, Bayesian-optimization style), max-of-smooth composites, constraints, global optimization (pp. 6, 20, 23).

method_links.note: Primary source for the tail bound on the estimated decrease, conditioned on the past. The SKILL paraphrase O(delta^-2q) holds for q in (1,2] with i.i.d. averaging. Workflow D should add the known eps_q bound, the theta threshold (3.1) and the CRN route O(Delta^-eps).

Step 5 says never go below the threshold, but the experiments run with theta = 0.5, far below the proven theta > 4 or about 9. This is disclosed, with a conjecture that smaller theta still converges in most cases. The threshold is on the acceptance constant, not on a probability.
One acceptance-test change (estimates plus power q) is carried through both the DS and the TR skeleton with the same proof.
Counts samples per iteration as a function of Delta_k, not evaluations to reach eps. There is no complexity bound, and the iteration-count trade-off for q -> 1 is left open.
Has a collection (96 problems x 10 runs), data and performance profiles, and the StoMADS baseline, but no solver release is mentioned.

transferable: Put the accuracy requirement on the quantity the acceptance test uses and scale it with the sufficient-decrease power q, so that the sample size falls with q (pp. 5-8).
Potential Phi_k = f - f* + eta*Delta^q plus a false-success loss bound handles successful and unsuccessful steps in one inequality (pp. 11-12).
Borel-Cantelli on the summable step sizes gives eventually small estimate errors, then run the deterministic Clarke argument on unsuccessful iterations (pp. 12-14).
Before claiming a weaker assumption, prove that each rival assumption implies it (p. 9).
Transfer a DS proof to TR through ||S_k|| >= rho*Delta_k from a Hessian bound (pp. 15-17).
Build profiles on the true f while solvers see noisy f; count repeated runs as separate problems (p. 19).
Report the gap between the theoretical and the tuned parameter in a numbered remark (p. 20).

quotes.text: This probabilistic condition focuses on the reduction estimate, that is the estimate of the difference between the function at the current iterate and at a potential next iterate, used in the acceptance test of those derivative-free algorithms.
Finding weaker versions of (3.1) that still guarantee convergence under reasonable assumptions remains of course an open problem to be studied more in depth in future works.

title: Bilevel optimization with a multi-objective lower-level problem: Risk-neutral and risk-averse formulations
contribution: New risk-neutral and risk-averse formulations (plus a stochastic version of the known optimistic one) for bilevel problems with a multi-objective lower level. Each comes with a bilevel stochastic (sub)gradient algorithm (BSG-OPT, BSG-RN, BSG-RA), obtained by treating the lower-level variable as a parameter.
problem_entry: An unfilled cell: lower-level multi-objective bilevel problems have received little attention deterministically and none from a stochastic approximation viewpoint. The ambiguity of 'min' over the lower-level Pareto set is the conceptual core (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Look at y as a parameter. Under strict convexity, parametrize the Pareto set by simplex weights. The optimistic reading makes the weights UL variables, risk-neutral averages over the weights (a companion problem, discretized and mini-batched), and risk-averse maximizes over the lifted set (y, lambda) with a Danskin/Fiacco subgradient. The BSG skeleton is kept throughout (pp. 3-13).
assumptions: f_u is C1 and the LL functions are C2. The LL objectives are strictly convex in y with P(x) nonempty, so weighted sums characterize P(x) exactly. y(x, lambda) exists and stochastic Hessian estimates are positive definite. Risk-averse additionally needs KKT and LICQ for (6.6) with P~(x) nonempty and compact. The LL is unconstrained and X is closed convex (pp. 2, 6-7, 12-13).
proof_devices: weighted-sum characterization of weak Pareto minimizers under convexity; strict convexity gives P = P_s (Prop. 3.1, p. 6)
equivalence of the optimistic BMOLL and a single-objective bilevel problem over (x, lambda), by contradiction (Prop. 4.1, p. 7)
adjoint gradient w.r.t. x and lambda by the implicit function theorem on sum_j lambda_j grad_y f_l^j = 0, with the mixed block equal to the stacked LL gradients (pp. 8, 10)
companion problem: expectation over weights lambda in the simplex instead of over P(x), discretized to N points and mini-batched (pp. 9-10)
lifting the Pareto set to (y, lambda) via weighted stationarity, with an equivalence result (Prop. 6.1, pp. 11-12)
Danskin-type subdifferential for a max over an x-dependent set (Fiacco Cor. 4.11) under KKT and LICQ (p. 12)
experiments: Python code on GitHub. Quadratic UL with JOS1, SP1 and a new GKV1 lower level; separable n=1, non-separable n=50, and stochastic with Gaussian noise on gradients and Hessians. Line search vs fixed step, Q-batch ablation with 95% CIs, 10 seeds. All methods solve Problems 1-3; BSG-RN is most robust to noise. No external baseline and no collection (pp. 13-19).
positioning: Reframes the deterministic weighted-sum work [1, 9, 29, 30] as 'the known optimistic formulation' and distinguishes Gu et al. [20] in detail. It builds on the group's BSG [19] and Liu-Vicente SMG [27]. Vicente's own 1994 and 2006 bilevel papers are not cited (pp. 3, 6, 21-23).
writing: The abstract names the gap then the contribution. Each formulation follows a fixed order: frozen-case intuition, formulation, equivalence proposition, gradient, algorithm box. Theory is deferred in one sentence, and extensions are built 'from known building blocks' (pp. 3, 5, 9, 11, 20).
limits_future: No convergence theory: the smooth cases are said to extend BSG, and the nonsmooth risk-averse theory is left for future work. Tests are small and synthetic. Future work: multi-objective UL via an adjoint multi-gradient QP, and both levels multi-objective, which needs further research for the risk-averse case (pp. 5, 13, 20-21).

method_links.note: The BSG skeleton is kept; only the objective and its gradient change with the reading (optimistic, risk-neutral, risk-averse). Extensions are assembled from known blocks.

Weighted-sum scalarization is used, but never with weights fixed a priori: the weights are variables, averaged over, or maximized over. Strict convexity makes the parametrization exact, so the missed-front risk is removed by assumption rather than by a dominance list.
No rates or counts; the theory is deferred to an extension of BSG, or to future work for the nonsmooth case.
Code is released, but there are only three synthetic problems, no collection, no profiles and no external baseline.

The development of the convergence theory for the non-smooth case (i.e., risk-averse formulation in Section 6) is left for future work.

title: Match score dataset for team ball sports
contribution: A dataset of 6115 match scores from major international men's competitions in 12 team ball sports. It was scraped from 161 Wikipedia pages, uses one six-field schema, has one CSV per sport, and is deposited at Mendeley Data.
problem_entry: A data gap: existing sports datasets cover few sports, cover leagues and college tournaments rather than international competitions, and use formats that differ by sport, which hampers cross-sport analysis (p. 2).
key_idea: One minimal common schema (Edition Year, Team 1, Team 2, Score 1, Score 2, Winner) defined formally with sets and a winner function, plus explicit scope and exclusion choices (pp. 2-4).
assumptions: Wikipedia is the source. The winner is defined by comparing scores, with Draw for ties. Cricket has no scores (the winner comes from Wikipedia, with No result/Match abandoned cases). How shoot-outs are recorded is not discussed (pp. 3, 5).
proof_devices: no proofs (data article)
formal set/tuple notation with a notation table fixing each CSV column (pp. 3-4)
experiments: None. Data collection is by Python web scraping. Tables show per-edition counts, which I checked sum to the Table 1 totals (6115). Undiscussed anomalies in the tables: Rugby 2007 has 8 matches, Soccer 2006 has 33 teams, one lacrosse row reads 45-71, and the DOI version (.2) differs from the URL (/1) (pp. 1, 3-4, 8-9).
positioning: Seven references (a sports-dataset list, parity/randomness studies, scoring dynamics, ML prediction, an umbrella review); no optimization literature (pp. 2, 5-6).
writing: Follows the Data in Brief template (specifications, value of the data, limitations, ethics, CRediT). Unusually for the genre, it defines the dataset with set notation (pp. 1-5).
limits_future: Stated limits: no cricket scores, and water polo 1987/1989/1991/1997 are missing. Intended uses (rankings, rating systems, prediction) are listed but not carried out (pp. 1-2, 5).

method_links.note: The released artefact is a dataset with a DOI rather than a solver: step 2 (make the collection available to others) as a stand-alone publication.

quotes.text: However, such datasets were compiled only for a reduced number of team ball sports, and they are different from our dataset because they cover professional leagues and collegiate tournaments rather than major international competitions.
Additionally, such datasets have different formats due to the specificity of each sport, posing challenges for cross-sport analyses.

title: Full-low evaluation methods for bound and linearly constrained derivative-free optimization
contribution: Extends full-low evaluation to bound and linear constraints. Full-Eval is projected FD-BFGS in the null space with an Armijo search abandoned when beta < gamma*alpha_k; Low-Eval is probabilistic feasible direct search in approximate tangent cones. The paper proves O(eps^-2) successful Full-Eval iterations and Clarke-Jahn stationarity, releases MATLAB code, and benchmarks on smooth, nonsmooth and noisy CUTEst-based sets.
problem_entry: An extension gap plus a practical constraint: FLE worked unconstrained, and simulation codes enforce hard bound/linear constraints that must hold for the simulation to run. FD quasi-Newton cost grows with n, while direct search is cheap and robust (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Keep Algorithm 1 of the unconstrained FLE unchanged (only a feasible x0 is required) and change only the step routines: projection for Full-Eval and approximate tangent cones for Low-Eval. The switching condition beta >= gamma*alpha_k ties the two step types together (pp. 5-7, 15-16).
assumptions: Smooth case: f bounded below, grad f L-Lipschitz, an angle/norm condition on directions, and gradient accuracy ||grad f - g|| <= u_g ||q^g|| with u_g < kappa(1-c) (new restriction); measure q(x) = ||P_F[x - grad f] - x||. Nonsmooth case: a forcing function, ||q^g|| > eps_g on successful Full-Eval iterations, bounded iterates, Lipschitz near x*, and refining directions dense in T(x*) (pp. 3, 7-8, 11-12).
proof_devices: lower bound beta_min on accepted backtracking steps from Taylor, the angle condition and gradient accuracy (Lemma 4.1, pp. 8-9)
telescoping over successful Full-Eval iterations only, dropping the other (monotone) iterations: at most ceil(L1 (f0 - flow) eps^-2) successful Full-Eval iterations (Thm 4.1, p. 10)
switching condition beta >= gamma*alpha_k turns Full-Eval decrease into c*kappa*gamma*eps_g^2*alpha_k/U_p; with rho(alpha_k) on Low-Eval, summability gives alpha_k -> 0 (Lemma 4.2, pp. 11-12)
Clarke-Jahn refining-direction argument on unsuccessful Low-Eval iterations (Thm 4.2, pp. 12-13)
criticality-step loop shrinking the FD parameter h until h <= u'_g ||q^h||, with finite termination via the FD error bound 0.5*sqrt(n)*L*h (Alg. 4, Prop. 4.1, pp. 13-14)
approximate tangent cones: steps of length <= xi along T(x, xi) remain feasible (Lemma 2.1, p. 5)
experiments: MATLAB code on GitHub. constFLE vs constBFGS (Full-Eval only), dspfd (Low-Eval only), NOMAD and patternsearch. Sets: 41 bound and 76 linear CUTEst problems (40 with inequalities), noisy multiplicative versions, l1-penalty nonsmooth versions (52 + 107), and 14 minimax problems. Performance profiles on evaluations, budget 100(n+1). FLE wins on smooth and l1 sets; it loses to NOMAD on minimax and to NOMAD/patternsearch on noisy sets (pp. 14-24).
positioning: Extends Berahas-Sohab-Vicente FLE and imports the Gratton-Royer-Vicente-Zhang dspfd. Draws on Lewis-Torczon / Kolda-Lewis-Torczon constraint handling and on FD quasi-Newton work (Berahas-Byrd-Nocedal, Shi et al.). Critiques are brief and practical: the FD cost, and NOMAD's handling of equality constraints (pp. 2, 4, 16, 19).
writing: The abstract frames a two-strategy trade-off and resolves it with a hybrid. The switching conditions are compared in a footnote, and the conclusion claims 'the best of both worlds' with 'overall suggest'. Loose ends: an inconsistent minimax ranking on p. 22 and mismatched figure captions on pp. 26-27 (pp. 1, 6, 22, 24).
limits_future: No evaluation complexity, explicitly out of scope. The nonsmooth result rests on an assumption about the run and on direction density. FLE loses on noisy and minimax sets. Future work: trust-region Full-Eval steps, one- or two-point feedback Low-Eval steps, and convex nonlinear constraints (pp. 11-12, 22-24).

method_links.note: The efficient FD-BFGS step runs freely in the Full-Eval role and convergence comes from direct search with a forcing function. The switching rule beta >= gamma*alpha_k is Method 1 Step 4 in another form. This is the constrained sequel of the FLE entry already in Method 1.
The framework is identical to unconstrained FLE; only feasibility handling changes (projection, approximate tangent cones).
Low-Eval uses probabilistic feasible descent, but the analysis assumes dense refining directions; the almost-sure guarantee is only cited from [22].
Counts successful Full-Eval iterations (O(eps^-2)); the evaluation count is declared outside the scope.
GitHub code, CUTEst-based collections in three regularity regimes, performance profiles, an ablation against each half plus external solvers, and losses reported.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: NOMAD best on minimax; NOMAD/patternsearch best on noisy sets; FLE between its halves on noisy bound-constrained problems.
A criticality-step loop on the FD parameter enforces the gradient-accuracy assumption in finitely many steps.
The number of unsuccessful Low-Eval attempts allowed equals the number of backtracks in the preceding Full-Eval.

transferable: In a hybrid, abandon the expensive step's line search once its step length falls below gamma times the cheap method's step size; both step types then give summable decreases in alpha_k (p. 6, pp. 11-12).
With linear equalities, take FD gradients along a null-space basis W (n - m evaluations) and use the direction -W H W^T g (p. 15).
Bound hybrid iterations by telescoping over the one step type with provable decrease and dropping the monotone others (p. 10).
Turn a gradient-accuracy assumption into a criticality loop on the FD parameter, with a finite-termination proposition (pp. 13-14).
Make nonsmooth test sets by moving constraints into an l1 penalty, penalizing only half the bounds (pp. 17-18).
Benchmark each component of a hybrid as its own solver (p. 17).

quotes.text: A key feature of our Full-Low Evaluation methodology that led to rigorous results (see the proof of Lemma 4.2) is to stop the line search once condition (3.3) is violated.
This difficulty already arises in the unconstrained setting [9], and accurately calculating such a bound falls outside the scope of this convergence analysis.
